objectClass.notes: Static monumental landmark building, exterior shell only. No interior geometry: a prop kit is only ever looked at from outside, so an interior costs draw calls, geometries and VRAM for something nobody sees. Nothing moves, so one root pivot and zero sockets is the correct contract. The ordination hall of a wat and its visual anchor. A stepped white terrace and plinth with a stair at each end; thirty red columns forming a peristyle round a solid white hall body with eight windows a side and a door at each end; a hipped portico skirt over the colonnade; a 45-degree middle roof layer; a top gable telescoped into three sections, centre highest; glazed eaves bands, white risers and bargeboards, red trim, carved gilt pediments in both end gables; sixteen curved horns; and eight bai sema boundary stones. The registry notes are explicit that the sema are what make this an ORDINATION hall rather than a general assembly hall, so they belong to the asset and are not optional dressing.

reasoning: The identity is the ROOF, and it is not a stack: a hipped portico skirt round the colonnade, a 45-degree middle layer the full 18 m of the core, and a top gable TELESCOPED along the length into a 12 m centre with its ridge at 14.8 m and two 3 m ends at 14.0 m -- read off the proxy's side elevation, where the layer lines run continuous and only the ridges step.
Five repetition systems: thirty columns, sixteen chofa and rake-foot horns, sixteen window surrounds, sixteen window leaves and eight boundary stones. Every one is instanced.

Material layering is seven -- stone, red lacquer, tile, olive glaze, gilt, shade and the carved pediment canvas -- because a Thai temple roof is genuinely polychrome, and four of them carry post-construction weathering canvases.
Action readiness is minimal: static landmark geometry, box collider, not breakable.

specDepthDecision.rationale: The roof cannot be expressed as nested full gables, and it cannot be expressed as one prism either: the layers step in plan on the SIDE slopes while the end gable is a single triangle from the middle layer's eaves to the ridge, and the ridge itself steps along the length. Each layer is therefore three solids -- a white riser, a glaze band, a tile field -- and the gable ends are their own slabs following the stacked outline.

silhouette.description: A stepped white platform to 1.30 m, a red colonnade to 6.6 m under a 37-degree portico skirt whose eaves are at 6.9 m, then the roof core: a 45-degree middle layer from 9.0 to 10.85 m and a top gable from 10.9 m whose ridge is 14.8 m over the 12 m centre and 14.0 m over each 3 m end, with the centre's gable faces showing 0.8 m above the end ridges. Horns at every gable apex (to 16.9 m), every rake foot and every skirt corner. The silhouette events are the colonnade's rhythm, the three roof registers, the telescoped ridge and the horns breaking every edge of the roofline.
silhouette.envelopeDerivation: x spans -6.95..+6.95 (the portico skirt's eaves fascia at hw 6.94 and the terrace at 6.85), z spans -12.00..+12.00 set by the bottom terrace, y spans 0.00 to 16.92 set by the tip of the centre-ridge chofa. The declaration was CHANGED for this rebuild: the first build was declared 12 x 12 x 24 and the Meshy proxy of the same plate normalises to long:h:short = 1 : 0.709 : 0.573, i.e. 24 x 17.0 x 13.7 m. The registry now declares 14 x 17 x 24, and every height here is read off the proxy's two orthographic elevations at that scale.
silhouette.meshyCrossCheck: Independent Meshy v7 reconstruction of the same plate normalises to long:h:short = 1 : 0.709 : 0.573. The first build was declared 1 : 0.5 : 0.5 and its area-weighted band comparison read mean |delta width| 0.173 and |delta depth| 0.446 of height -- the largest divergence of the monumental set, almost all of it that one ratio. This rebuild re-declares the envelope from the proxy and reads every register off its orthographic elevations (scratch/_mon/front.mjs, side and end): skirt eaves hw 6.8, middle eaves hw 5.0 at 9.0 m, top eaves hw 3.1 at 10.9 m, ridges 14.8 / 14.0 m, apex chofa to 17.0 m. The band table now reads mean |delta width| 0.017 and |delta depth| 0.044 of height, and the one band over 0.05 is band 4 (6.8-8.5 m), where the proxy's skirt eaves fascia is taller than the 0.4 m built here.

placement.note: Centred on each surround, standing 0.03 m proud of it.

featureReviews.evidence: A hipped 37-degree portico skirt, a 45-degree middle layer the full 18 m, and a top gable telescoped into a 12 m centre at 14.8 m and two 3 m ends at 14.0 m, each register a white riser, a glaze band and a tile field; white bargeboards with red strips; sixteen curved horns; one carved pediment per end gable.
featureReviews.notes: The first build nested three same-length tiers concentrically -- a wedding cake, not a Thai roof -- which is the structure the user returned. The proxy's side elevation shows the layer lines continuous along the length with only the ridges stepping, and its end elevation shows one gable triangle from the middle eaves to the ridge, so the end sections' top pitch is the middle layer's 45 degrees continued and the top layer's step shows only on the side slopes. The centre section's gable faces at z = +-6 show 0.8 m above the end ridges, which is the telescoped step the plate shows behind the near pediment. The skirt is quad-strip rings because it hips round the ends and no extrusion can do that; it closes with a soffit and an inner wall so the turntable gate cannot read through it.

featureReviews.evidence: Seven materials at PBR confidence 0.735-0.860, every albedo measured off the plate, and four seamless Canvas 2D weathering tiles bound post-construction: streaked whitewash, peeling lacquer, laid tile courses with moss, and a carved gilt pediment. 4 textures, 5.3 MB, 68 ms.

Dark cores are held at 0.62 of clean for the luma-58 hole gate.

lodPlan.strategy: full component tree and material layers
merge static components and reduce local feature geometry

performanceBudget.optimizationPolicy: Real-time browser FPS prop on low-end integrated GPUs; a level builder places hundreds at once. All four ceilings come from thaikit resolveBudget() for the hero4x class and none was invented. The component split was costed against the DRAW-CALL ceiling in the blockout, before any geometry existed: parts that share a material are merged into one component rather than left to be merged later, because a pivot hung off a part cannot be merged afterwards.

drawCalls.note: Ten components and five repetition systems: 15 of 24. The columns are the expensive lesson avoided -- thirty of them would exceed the draw-call budget on their own -- and the sixteen windows would have doubled the count again as separate meshes.

materials.note: stone covers the platform, the body, the risers, the gable walls, the bargeboards, the window surrounds AND the boundary stones; red covers the columns and all the trim; gilt the sixteen horns; carved the four pediments. Seven of sixteen materials, and the seven are genuinely seven finishes -- a Thai temple roof is polychrome by construction.

uniqueGeometries.note: One per component plus one per repetition system. A scaled box is NOT a shared geometry -- the generator bakes real dimensions in via geometry.scale(), so every differently-sized box is genuinely distinct. Each InstancedMesh reuses a single geometry across all its instances, which is the whole point.

triangles.note: 3,992 of 32,000. Prisms, quad strips and boxes, with the horns as nine-segment curves; nothing here is expensive. The tile course and the pediment carving that the first build declared lost to the budget are both here, as canvases costing no triangles at all.

lightingFromPhoto.notes: The plate is a flat studio lightbox: surfaces at 90 degrees to each other measure within a few levels, which is only possible under near-shadowless illumination. That is WHY the measured crop means are usable as albedo with little correction.
High fill ratio inferred from the shadow-side wall retaining full value.

The seamless backdrop acts as a large uniform environment. The thaikit harness supplies NO environment map, which is why every metal on this prop carries a metalness well below its physical value -- a metal with nothing to reflect renders black.
NO rim light in the plate. Recorded so a missing rim in the render is not read as a defect.
Exposure 1.0 with ACES filmic tone mapping; no exposure compensation is applied to the measured albedos and none is warranted.

NO contact or ground shadow in the plate -- it is a cut-out against a seamless backdrop. Recorded so the absence is not read as a missing feature. IN USE this is a floor-placed building and the HOST scene owns its contact shadow: castShadow ships enabled on every mesh and the factory defines no ground plane of its own.

proceduralStrategy.strategy: Extruded prisms, quad-strip rings, and boxes rotated to the rake. The roof is the interesting case: a hipped skirt has to be a ring of trapezoids because an extrusion gives vertical ends; the layers above it are truncated gable cross-sections extruded along the hall, with the top gable cut into three extrusions of different ridge height so the roof telescopes.

Five InstancedMesh systems carry 86 of the prop's 132 discrete parts. The horn system uses a per-instance yaw, a per-instance rise and a NEGATIVE X scale for the opposite hand, which is what lets one geometry serve every apex, rake foot and hip corner.
All procedural variation is assigned by instance INDEX, never from a random source, so the model is byte-identical on every build.

Every material is declared textureless, and four seamless Canvas 2D tiles are bound AFTER construction as map and bumpMap: streaked whitewash on the stone, peeling lacquer on the red (re-based to the plaster envelope so the flakes can be brighter than the base), laid tile courses with moss on the terracotta and the glaze, and the carved gilt pediment. Every tone is a measured display-space ratio; dark cores are held above the hole gate; the whole set builds in under 70 ms and 5.3 MB of texture VRAM.
